doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

chapter: Record hunting and the Air Force
title: Junk-shopping for 78s, including Washington, D.C.
summary: Hunting rare records was hard work; he found Dodds and Keppard records while stationed in Washington, going door to door.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: You know there it is, I would have killed for those records and you just click on them. How were you going to get them?
Did it make it more precious for you?
Because it was something you had to really aspire to get and figure out how to get and carry the 78s home and all that stuff.

Oh yeah. Junk shopping I remember I was in Washington, D.C. I went to the Army Air Corps, which became the Air Force just as I left, band school. In Bolling Field. And my uncle, Uncle John, the musical one, lived there and his wife was a nurse there at St. Elizabeth or something. And Anacostia was there, the big black neighborhood. And I remember one day I went out and it was unbelievable, there were like rarity, like treasures. God I went out and I found a Johnny Dodds Paramount record in very good shape. You could see Dixieland Thumpers and I found a Freddie Keppard record. I mean, and it was a gold mine. And New York had been picked out. There were a lot of big collectors here you know, they had been picked out and were very hard to find anymore. But I did, I even went door to door, you know in the black neighborhoods in the afternoon, “I’m looking for old records, have you any old records?” Sometimes I found them.
